claim: Human embryo polarization occurs in two steps: it begins with the apical enrichment of F-actin and is followed by the apical accumulation of the PAR complex.
source: Here, we show that human embryo polarization occurs in two steps: it begins with the apical enrichment of F-actin and is followed by the apical accumulation of the PAR complex.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing temporal separation of F-actin and PARD6 polarization in human embryos at different developmental time points (Figure 1e-g).

claim: Two-step polarization process leads to the formation of an apical domain at the 8–16 cell stage in human embryos.
source: This two-step polarization process leads to the formation of an apical domain at the 8–16 cell stage.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging and immunofluorescence data showing polarization occurring during the 8-16 cell stage transition (Figure 1).

claim: Apical domain formation requires Phospholipase C (PLC) signaling, specifically the enzymes PLCB1 and PLCE1, from the eight-cell stage onwards.
source: Using RNA interference, we show that apical domain formation requires Phospholipase C (PLC) signaling, specifically the enzymes PLCB1 and PLCE1, from the eight-cell stage onwards.
evidence: Supported by RNAi experiments showing reduced F-actin and PARD6 polarization after PLCB1 and PLCE1 knockdown (Figure 2).

claim: Expression of GATA3 can be initiated independently of embryo polarization.
source: Finally, we show that although expression of the critical TE differentiation marker GATA3 can be initiated independently of embryo polarization, downregulation of PLCB1 and PLCE1 decreases GATA3 expression through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing GATA3 expression in both polarized and non-polarized cells (Figure 3a-c).

claim: Downregulation of PLCB1 and PLCE1 decreases GATA3 expression through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
source: Finally, we show that although expression of the critical TE differentiation marker GATA3 can be initiated independently of embryo polarization, downregulation of PLCB1 and PLCE1 decreases GATA3 expression through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
evidence: Supported by RNAi experiments showing decreased GATA3 expression specifically in unpolarized cells after PLCB1/PLCE1 knockdown (Figure 3d-f).

claim: Apical domain formation reinforces a TE fate.
source: Therefore, apical domain formation reinforces a TE fate.
evidence: Inferred from data showing higher GATA3 and YAP1 expression in polarized cells compared to unpolarized cells (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c).

claim: The trophectoderm (TE) will generate the placenta.
source: Three lineages have to become established by the time of embryo implantation: the trophectoderm (TE), which will generate the placenta, the epiblast (EPI), which will form the embryo proper, and the hypoblast, which will form the yolk sac (Shahbazi and Zernicka-Goetz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The epiblast (EPI) will form the embryo proper.
source: Three lineages have to become established by the time of embryo implantation: the trophectoderm (TE), which will generate the placenta, the epiblast (EPI), which will form the embryo proper, and the hypoblast, which will form the yolk sac (Shahbazi and Zernicka-Goetz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The hypoblast will form the yolk sac.
source: Three lineages have to become established by the time of embryo implantation: the trophectoderm (TE), which will generate the placenta, the epiblast (EPI), which will form the embryo proper, and the hypoblast, which will form the yolk sac (Shahbazi and Zernicka-Goetz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: In the mouse embryo, the physical process of lineage segregation begins upon embryo compaction and polarization at the late eight-cell stage, the beginning of day 3 of development.
source: Studies in the mouse embryo showed that the physical process of lineage segregation begins upon embryo compaction and polarization at the late eight-cell stage, the beginning of day 3 of development.
evidence: Supported by citations to mouse embryo studies.

claim: The processes of embryo compaction and polarization lead to the closer apposition of neighboring blastomeres and the formation of an apical domain that orients towards the outside of the embryo.
source: The processes of embryo compaction and polarization lead to the closer apposition of neighboring blastomeres and the formation of an apical domain that orients towards the outside of the embryo (Cockburn and Rossant, 2010; Fleming and Johnson, 1988; White et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on embryo development.

claim: The differential inheritance of the apical domain during the successive cleavage divisions generates polarized and non-polarized cells that sort to the outside and inside of the embryo, respectively.
source: The differential inheritance of the apical domain during the successive cleavage divisions generates polarized and non-polarized cells that sort to the outside and inside of the embryo, respectively (Anani et al., 2014; Johnson and Ziomek, 1981; Samarage et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on cell sorting in embryos.

claim: Cell polarity and cell position will regulate the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors.
source: Subsequently, cell polarity and cell position will regulate the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors, and consequently, the outer polarized cells will differentiate into TE, and inner non-polarized cells will retain pluripotency and become the inner cell mass (ICM), which will give rise to the EPI and hypoblast lineages (Chazaud and Yamanaka, 2016; Zhu and Zernicka-Goetz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lineage specification.

claim: Outer polarized cells will differentiate into TE.
source: Subsequently, cell polarity and cell position will regulate the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors, and consequently, the outer polarized cells will differentiate into TE, and inner non-polarized cells will retain pluripotency and become the inner cell mass (ICM), which will give rise to the EPI and hypoblast lineages (Chazaud and Yamanaka, 2016; Zhu and Zernicka-Goetz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lineage specification.

claim: Inner non-polarized cells will retain pluripotency and become the inner cell mass (ICM).
source: Subsequently, cell polarity and cell position will regulate the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors, and consequently, the outer polarized cells will differentiate into TE, and inner non-polarized cells will retain pluripotency and become the inner cell mass (ICM), which will give rise to the EPI and hypoblast lineages (Chazaud and Yamanaka, 2016; Zhu and Zernicka-Goetz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lineage specification.

claim: The ICM will give rise to the EPI and hypoblast lineages.
source: Subsequently, cell polarity and cell position will regulate the expression of lineage-specific transcription factors, and consequently, the outer polarized cells will differentiate into TE, and inner non-polarized cells will retain pluripotency and become the inner cell mass (ICM), which will give rise to the EPI and hypoblast lineages (Chazaud and Yamanaka, 2016; Zhu and Zernicka-Goetz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lineage specification.

claim: Previous studies indicated that compaction of human embryos takes place between days 3 and 4 after fertilization.
source: Previous studies indicated that compaction of human embryos takes place between days 3 and 4 after fertilization (Iwata et al., 2014; Nikas et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on human embryo compaction.

claim: A total of 260 supernumerary in vitro fertilized human embryos that were cryopreserved at embryonic day 3 were analyzed.
source: To determine the timing of cell polarization in the human embryo, we carried out detailed analyses on a total of 260 supernumerary in vitro fertilized human embryos that were cryopreserved at embryonic day 3.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental sample size.

claim: At the start of the experiment, embryos had a mean number of eight cells that increased to approximately 12 cells after 24 hr in culture.
source: At the start of the experiment, embryos had a mean number of eight cells that increased to approximately 12 cells after 24 hr in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-d.

claim: The cell cycle time decreased from the 4–8 cell stage transition (22.15 hours) to the 8–16 cell stage transition (14.49 hr).
source: Our analyses revealed that the cell cycle time decreased from the 4–8 cell stage transition (22.15 hours) to the 8–16 cell stage transition (14.49 hr) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The majority of analyzed embryos (89.4%, N = 132) showed no signs of degenerated cells after warming.
source: The majority of analyzed embryos (89.4%, N = 132) showed no signs of degenerated cells, both after warming (89.4%, N = 132; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) and after 24 hr of culture (95.3%, N = 85; Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), indicating embryo quality was not compromised during the experiments.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: 95.3% of analyzed embryos (N = 85) showed no signs of degenerated cells after 24 hr of culture.
source: The majority of analyzed embryos (89.4%, N = 132) showed no signs of degenerated cells, both after warming (89.4%, N = 132; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) and after 24 hr of culture (95.3%, N = 85; Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), indicating embryo quality was not compromised during the experiments.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Embryo quality was not compromised during the experiments.
source: The majority of analyzed embryos (89.4%, N = 132) showed no signs of degenerated cells, both after warming (89.4%, N = 132; Figure 1—figure supplement 1f) and after 24 hr of culture (95.3%, N = 85; Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), indicating embryo quality was not compromised during the experiments.
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of degenerated cells observed.

claim: The average cell number in the embryo at the start of compaction was 10.14 (N = 83).
source: In this way, we were able to reveal that the average cell number in the embryo at the start of compaction was 10.14 (N = 83), increasing to 11.57 (N = 54) by completion of compaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: The average cell number in the embryo at completion of compaction was 11.57 (N = 54).
source: In this way, we were able to reveal that the average cell number in the embryo at the start of compaction was 10.14 (N = 83), increasing to 11.57 (N = 54) by completion of compaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: The beginning of compaction was accomplished on average 78.2 ± 6.6 hours post-fertilization.
source: These analyses revealed that the beginning of compaction was accomplished on average 78.2 ± 6.6 hours post-fertilization, while the completion of compaction was accomplished at 80.2 ± 8.5 hr (Figure 1 b – d ; Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data from embryos with known fertilization times (Figure 1b-d).

claim: The completion of compaction was accomplished at 80.2 ± 8.5 hr post-fertilization.
source: These analyses revealed that the beginning of compaction was accomplished on average 78.2 ± 6.6 hours post-fertilization, while the completion of compaction was accomplished at 80.2 ± 8.5 hr (Figure 1 b – d ; Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data from embryos with known fertilization times (Figure 1b-d).

claim: The onset of compaction in human embryos is heterogeneous.
source: These observations indicate that the onset of compaction in human embryos is heterogeneous, and while compaction starts at the eight-cell stage, it extends to the 8–16 cell stage transition.
evidence: Inferred from the variability in compaction timing observed across embryos.

claim: Compaction starts at the eight-cell stage in human embryos.
source: These observations indicate that the onset of compaction in human embryos is heterogeneous, and while compaction starts at the eight-cell stage, it extends to the 8–16 cell stage transition.
evidence: Supported by cell number quantification at compaction initiation.

claim: Compaction extends to the 8–16 cell stage transition in human embryos.
source: These observations indicate that the onset of compaction in human embryos is heterogeneous, and while compaction starts at the eight-cell stage, it extends to the 8–16 cell stage transition.
evidence: Supported by cell number quantification at compaction completion.

claim: The timing of compaction in human embryos is consistent with previous observations.
source: This finding is consistent with previous observations on human embryos (Iwata et al., 2014; Nikas et al., 1996; Skiadas et al., 2006) and contrasts with observations on mouse embryos where compaction is completed by the end of the eight-cell stage (Levy et al., 1986; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on human embryo compaction.

claim: In mouse embryos, compaction is completed by the end of the eight-cell stage.
source: This finding is consistent with previous observations on human embryos (Iwata et al., 2014; Nikas et al., 1996; Skiadas et al., 2006) and contrasts with observations on mouse embryos where compaction is completed by the end of the eight-cell stage (Levy et al., 1986; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mouse embryo compaction.

claim: In the mouse embryo, the localization of the PAR complex to the apical domain serves as the crucial developmental transition that controls embryo polarization and the expression of TE lineage-specific transcription factors.
source: In the mouse embryo, the localization of the PAR complex to the apical domain serves as the crucial developmental transition that controls embryo polarization and the expression of TE lineage-specific transcription factors (Sasaki, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on mouse embryo polarization.

claim: PAR complex components, such as PARD6, are expressed in human embryos at the eight-cell stage.
source: Transcriptomic analyses of human embryos indicate that PAR complex components, such as PARD6, are also expressed in human embryos at the eight-cell stage (Petropoulos et al., 2016; Stirparo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: None of the embryos were compacted after 2 hr of culture (N = 18 embryos).
source: We found that none of the embryos were compacted after 2 hr of culture, in agreement with our time-lapse studies above (N = 18 embryos).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: At 2 hr post-warming, both cortical F-actin and PARD6 were uniformly distributed within the embryos.
source: At this stage, both cortical F-actin and PARD6 were uniformly distributed within the embryos, indicating that they had not yet initiated polarization (N = 135 blastomeres; 17 embryos) (Figure 1 e–g).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: At 2 hr post-warming, embryos had not yet initiated polarization.
source: At this stage, both cortical F-actin and PARD6 were uniformly distributed within the embryos, indicating that they had not yet initiated polarization (N = 135 blastomeres; 17 embryos) (Figure 1 e–g).
evidence: Inferred from the uniform distribution of polarization markers.

claim: After 9 hr of culture, 26% of embryos had become fully compacted (N = 199 blastomeres; 19 embryos).
source: However, 7 hr later, we found that 26% of embryos had become fully compacted (N = 199 blastomeres; 19 embryos).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: All compacted blastomeres displayed an apical enrichment of cortical F-actin at the cell-contact free surface.
source: All compacted blastomeres displayed an apical enrichment of cortical F-actin at the cell-contact free surface (Figure 1e –g).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: Only half of compacted blastomeres showed PARD6 polarization at 9 hr post-warming (26.3%, N = 199 blastomeres; 20 embryos).
source: In contrast, only half of these compacted blastomeres showed PARD6 polarization (26.3%, N = 199 blastomeres; 20 embryos) (Figure 1e –g).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: The proportion of compacted embryos in which both F-actin and PARD6 were polarized increased significantly during the next 15 hr of culture (91.0% for F-actin and 71.5% for PARD6 polarization; 32 embryos).
source: The proportion of compacted embryos in which both F-actin and PARD6 were polarized increased significantly during the next 15 hr of culture (91.0% for F-actin and 71.5% for PARD6 polarization; 32 embryos) (Figure 1e –g).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: None of the embryos showed F-actin nor PARD6 polarization at 74–75 hours post-fertilization (N = 49 blastomeres; six embryos).
source: Specifically, none of the embryos showed F-actin nor PARD6 polarization (N = 49 blastomeres; six embryos) at 74–75 hours post-fertilization.
evidence: Direct observation from embryos with known fertilization times.

claim: F-actin polarization was detected at 77–80 hours post-fertilization (57.1 %; N = 21 blastomeres; two embryos).
source: We were able to detect F-actin polarization at 77–80 hours post-fertilization (57.1 %; N = 21 blastomeres; two embryos), and PARD6 at 93–97 hours post-fertilization (41.4%; N = 99 blastomeres; nine embryos) (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1h-i.

claim: PARD6 polarization was detected at 93–97 hours post-fertilization (41.4%; N = 99 blastomeres; nine embryos).
source: We were able to detect F-actin polarization at 77–80 hours post-fertilization (57.1 %; N = 21 blastomeres; two embryos), and PARD6 at 93–97 hours post-fertilization (41.4%; N = 99 blastomeres; nine embryos) (Figure 1h–i).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1h-i.

claim: The level of PARD6 apical enrichment is positively correlated with embryo cell numbers.
source: The level of PARD6 apical enrichment, the size of the PARD6 domain, and the number of blastomeres showing PARD6 polarization were positively correlated with embryo cell numbers, indicating that the apical localization of PARD6 increases as embryos develop in culture (Figure 1j –k and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1j-k.

claim: The size of the PARD6 domain is positively correlated with embryo cell numbers.
source: The level of PARD6 apical enrichment, the size of the PARD6 domain, and the number of blastomeres showing PARD6 polarization were positively correlated with embryo cell numbers, indicating that the apical localization of PARD6 increases as embryos develop in culture (Figure 1j –k and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1j-k.

claim: The number of blastomeres showing PARD6 polarization is positively correlated with embryo cell numbers.
source: The level of PARD6 apical enrichment, the size of the PARD6 domain, and the number of blastomeres showing PARD6 polarization were positively correlated with embryo cell numbers, indicating that the apical localization of PARD6 increases as embryos develop in culture (Figure 1j –k and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1j-k and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j.

claim: The apical localization of PARD6 increases as embryos develop in culture.
source: The level of PARD6 apical enrichment, the size of the PARD6 domain, and the number of blastomeres showing PARD6 polarization were positively correlated with embryo cell numbers, indicating that the apical localization of PARD6 increases as embryos develop in culture (Figure 1j –k and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between PARD6 localization and cell number.

claim: aPKC localized to the cell-contact free surface at the same developmental time frame as PARD6 (N = 62 blastomeres; four embryos).
source: We found that aPKC localized to the cell-contact free surface at the same developmental time frame (N = 62 blastomeres; four embryos) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1k).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1k.

claim: The process of human embryo polarization follows two steps: in the first step, F-actin becomes polarized concomitantly with embryo compaction, and in the second step, the PAR complex becomes polarized.
source: Together, these results indicate that the process of human embryo polarization follows two steps: in the first step, F-actin becomes polarized and this happens concomitantly with embryo compaction, and in the second step, the PAR complex becomes polarized.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal separation of F-actin and PAR complex polarization observed in the data.

claim: The onset of embryo polarization in the mouse embryo is driven by the PLC-Protein Kinase C (PKC) pathway.
source: Our recent study in the mouse embryo showed that the onset of embryo polarization is driven by the PLC-Protein Kinase C (PKC) pathway, which enables the recruitment of the actin-myosin complex to the cell membrane (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mouse embryo polarization.

claim: The PLC-PKC pathway enables the recruitment of the actin-myosin complex to the cell membrane in mouse embryos.
source: Our recent study in the mouse embryo showed that the onset of embryo polarization is driven by the PLC-Protein Kinase C (PKC) pathway, which enables the recruitment of the actin-myosin complex to the cell membrane (Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mouse embryo polarization.

claim: Treatment with either 5 μM or 7.5 μM U73122 did not have an obvious effect on embryo cell numbers.
source: Treatment with either 5 μM or 7.5 μM U73122 did not have an obvious effect on embryo cell numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: High levels of PLC inhibitor (10 μM) affected embryo development.
source: By contrast, high levels of PLC inhibitor (10 μM) affected embryo development (N = 66 control; N = 23 35 mM DMSO; N = 31 5 μM U73122; N = 20 53 mM DMSO; N = 20 7.5 μM U73122; N = 9 70 mM DMSO; and N = 10 10 μM U73122-treated embryos, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both 5 μM and 7.5 μM U73122 significantly reduced the apical enrichment of F-actin when compared to control embryos.
source: We found that both 5 μM and 7.5 μM U73122 significantly reduced the apical enrichment of F-actin when compared to control embryos (N = 39 control embryos; N = 13 5 μM U73122-treated embryos; N = 23 7.5 μM U73122-treated embryos).
evidence: Supported by quantification data from immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: When compared to the DMSO vehicle control, the difference in F-actin apical enrichment after U73122 treatment was not statistically significant.
source: However, when compared to the DMSO vehicle control the difference was not statistically significant (N = 7 35 mM DMSO-treated embryos; N = 15 53 mM DMSO-treated embryos) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: The apical enrichment of PARD6 was not significantly different when U73122-treated embryos were compared to the DMSO vehicle control.
source: Similarly, the apical enrichment of PARD6 was not significantly different when U73122-treated embryos were compared to the DMSO vehicle control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: PLCE1 and PLCB1 expression levels rank the highest among all functional PLC isoforms in human embryos between the two- to the eight-cell stage.
source: Specifically, we depleted PLCE1 and PLCB1, as we found that their expression levels rank the highest among all functional PLC isoforms in human embryos between the two- to the eight-cell stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2aYan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by expression profile data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and citation to Yan et al., 2013.

claim: siRNA injection resulted in a 71% downregulation of PLCE1.
source: These experiments revealed a 71% and 90% downregulation of PLCE1 and PLCB1 respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: siRNA injection resulted in a 90% downregulation of PLCB1.
source: These experiments revealed a 71% and 90% downregulation of PLCE1 and PLCB1 respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The number of polarized cells in PLCE1/PLCB1 siRNA embryos was significantly reduced after depletion of PLCE1/PLCB1.
source: The number of polarized cells and apical enrichment of PARD6 and in PLCE1/PLCB1 siRNA embryos was significantly reduced after depletion of PLCE1/PLCB1 (N = 17 control siRNA embryos; N = 12 PLCB1+ PLCE1 siRNA embryos) (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Apical enrichment of PARD6 in PLCE1/PLCB1 siRNA embryos was significantly reduced after depletion of PLCE1/PLCB1.
source: The number of polarized cells and apical enrichment of PARD6 and in PLCE1/PLCB1 siRNA embryos was significantly reduced after depletion of PLCE1/PLCB1 (N = 17 control siRNA embryos; N = 12 PLCB1+ PLCE1 siRNA embryos) (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Both U73122 treatment and PLCE1+ PLCB1 siRNA led to a mild and non-statistically significant effect on compaction.
source: Both U73122 treatment and PLCE1+ PLCB1 siRNA led to a mild and non-statistically significant effect on compaction (N = 66 control; N = 23 35 mM DMSO; N = 31 5 μM U73122; N = 27 53 mM DMSO; N = 27 7.5 μM U73122; N = 14 control siRNA; and N = 13 PLCE1+ PLCB1 siRNA-injected embryos. Figure 2—figure supplement 2c-d).
evidence: Supported by compaction analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c-d.

claim: PLC signaling is required for the establishment of cell polarity in the human embryo.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that PLC signaling is required for the establishment of cell polarity in the human embryo.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in polarization markers after PLC inhibition and knockdown.

claim: The impairment of F-actin polarization upon PLC inhibition did not significantly compromise embryo compaction.
source: Interestingly, the impairment of F-actin polarization upon PLC inhibition did not significantly compromise embryo compaction.
evidence: Supported by compaction analysis after PLC inhibition.

claim: Alternative pathways to F-actin-mediated cortical tension might be sufficient to drive compaction in the human embryo.
source: Our results, therefore, suggest that alternative pathways to F-actin-mediated cortical tension might be sufficient to drive compaction in the human embryo, which should be further tested in future studies.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observation that compaction occurs despite F-actin polarization impairment.

claim: GATA3 is a key marker of TE specification that is already expressed at the compacting morula stage in human embryos.
source: To address this question, we analyzed the spatiotemporal expression of the transcription factor GATA3, a key marker of TE specification that is already expressed at the compacting morula stage in human embryos (Petropoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to transcriptomic study.

claim: There was no expression of GATA3 in human embryos after either 2 or 9 hr in culture, regardless of whether individual cells within the embryo were polarized or not.
source: We found no expression of GATA3 in human embryos after either 2 or 9 hr in culture, regardless of whether individual cells within the embryo were polarized or not (Figure 3a–b, N = 135 blastomeres; 17 embryos for 2 hr and N = 199 blastomeres; 20 embryos for 9 hr).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: GATA3 expression became visible in 53.5% of blastomeres after 24 hr of culture, on day 4.
source: In contrast, GATA3 expression became visible in 53.5% of blastomeres after 24 hr of culture, on day 4 (Figure 3a–b, N = 519 blastomeres; 33 embryos).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: GATA3 was expressed in both polarized and non-polarized blastomeres even at the early blastocyst stage.
source: Remarkably, we found that GATA3 was expressed in both polarized and non-polarized blastomeres even at the early blastocyst stage, although the nuclear signal intensity of GATA3 was significantly higher in polarized cells (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The nuclear signal intensity of GATA3 was significantly higher in polarized cells.
source: Remarkably, we found that GATA3 was expressed in both polarized and non-polarized blastomeres even at the early blastocyst stage, although the nuclear signal intensity of GATA3 was significantly higher in polarized cells (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In the mouse, Gata3 expression becomes downregulated in the ICM at the early blastocyst stage.
source: This is in contrast to the mouse, in which Gata3 expression becomes downregulated in the ICM at the early blastocyst stage (Ralston et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on mouse Gata3 expression.

claim: In human embryos, regulation of GATA3 expression might be initiated independently of embryo polarization, but reinforced by the acquisition of apicobasal polarity.
source: These results suggest that in human embryos regulation of GATA3 expression might be initiated independently of embryo polarization, but reinforced by the acquisition of apicobasal polarity (Figure 3a–c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA3 is expressed in both polarized and unpolarized cells, but at higher levels in polarized cells.

claim: YAP1 was significantly enriched in polarized cells in comparison to unpolarized cells (N = 38 blastomeres; four embryos).
source: We found that YAP1 was significantly enriched in polarized cells in comparison to unpolarized cells (N = 38 blastomeres; four embryos) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Cell polarization promotes the expression of TE-associated transcription factors at the morula stage but it is not essential for the initiation of their expression.
source: These results suggest that cell polarization promotes the expression of TE-associated transcription at the morula stage but it is not essential for the initiation of their expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TE markers are expressed in unpolarized cells but at lower levels than in polarized cells.

claim: Treatment with 7.5 μM U73122 led to a significant reduction of the nuclear GATA3 signal intensity when compared to control medium and 53 mM DMSO vehicle control.
source: We found that treatment with 7.5 μM U73122 led to a significant reduction of the nuclear GATA3 signal intensity when compared to control medium and 53 mM DMSO vehicle control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e), N = 142 control blastomeres; N = 37 35 mM DMSO blastomeres; N = 84 53 mM DMSO blastomeres; N = 56 5 μM U73122 blastomeres; and N = 90 7.5 μM U73122 blastomeres.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Depletion of PLCB1 and PLCE1 by siRNA led to a significant reduction of GATA3 expression.
source: In agreement with the U73122 treatment results, depletion of PLCB1 and PLCE1 by siRNA also led to a significant reduction of GATA3 expression (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3d-e.

claim: The decrease in GATA3 expression after PLCB1 and PLCE1 siRNA was specific to unpolarized cells.
source: By classifying blastomeres according to their polarity status, we observed that the decrease in GATA3 expression was specific to unpolarized cells (Figure 3f), and hence the effect of PLCB1 and PLCE1 siRNA on GATA3 expression is through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The effect of PLCB1 and PLCE1 siRNA on GATA3 expression is through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
source: By classifying blastomeres according to their polarity status, we observed that the decrease in GATA3 expression was specific to unpolarized cells (Figure 3f), and hence the effect of PLCB1 and PLCE1 siRNA on GATA3 expression is through a reduction in the number of polarized cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA3 reduction is specific to unpolarized cells.

claim: The onset of GATA3 is controlled by a polarity-independent pathway.
source: Together, these results suggest that the onset of GATA3 is controlled by a polarity-independent pathway, but the levels of nuclear GATA3 are reinforced by a polarity-dependent pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA3 is expressed in unpolarized cells.

claim: The levels of nuclear GATA3 are reinforced by a polarity-dependent pathway.
source: Together, these results suggest that the onset of GATA3 is controlled by a polarity-independent pathway, but the levels of nuclear GATA3 are reinforced by a polarity-dependent pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA3 levels are higher in polarized cells.

claim: In the mouse embryo, inner cells are produced after all blastomeres become polarized at the eight-cell stage and by subsequent cell divisions from the 8- to 16-cell stage.
source: In the mouse embryo, inner cells are produced after all blastomeres become polarized at the eight-cell stage and by subsequent cell divisions from the 8- to 16-cell stage.
evidence: Statement about mouse embryo development based on established knowledge.

claim: In mouse embryos, inner cells can only be observed in embryos having more than eight polarized cells.
source: Consequently, inner cells can only be observed in embryos having more than eight polarized cells.
evidence: Logical inference from the mechanism of inner cell generation in mouse embryos.

claim: In 37% of human embryos, inner cells were present with less than eight outer polarized cells (N = 21 embryos).
source: Remarkably, we found that in 37% of human embryos, inner cells were present with less than eight outer polarized cells (Figure 4a–b, N = 21 embryos).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: The generation of inner cells in the human embryo might not require the preceding establishment of embryo polarization.
source: This suggests that the generation of inner cells in the human embryo might not require the preceding establishment of embryo polarization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inner cells are present before full polarization.

claim: The size of inner cells in human embryos was highly variable, ranging from 229.123 to 1896.4 μm2.
source: In addition, we found that the size of inner cells was highly variable, ranging from 229.123 to 1896.4 μm2 (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: The size of eight-cell stage blastomeres ranges from 895.432 to 2627.03 μm2.
source: This partially overlapped with the size of eight-cell stage blastomeres, which ranges from 895.432 to 2627.03 μm2 (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 4d.

claim: In 34% (18 out of 53) of the embryos examined, inner cells were bigger than the smallest eight-cell stage blastomere.
source: We found that in 34% (18 out of 53) of the embryos we examined, inner cells were bigger than the smallest eight-cell stage blastomere.
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements and comparison.

claim: Cells might be internalized without undertaking asymmetric cell division at the 8- to 16-cell stage transition in human embryos.
source: This result suggests cells might be internalized without undertaking asymmetric cell division at the 8- to 16-cell stage transition.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some inner cells are larger than expected from asymmetric division.

claim: A blastomere became internalized during the process of embryo compaction in at least one observed case.
source: Our time-lapse recordings, allowed us to observe a case in which a blastomere became internalized during the process of embryo compaction (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4e.

claim: At least some cells are allocated to the ICM independently of the cell divisions of the eight-cell stage blastomeres in the human embryo.
source: Although we could only fluorescently label a small number of human embryos to record the spatial localization and size of cells, our results suggest that at least some cells are allocated to the ICM independently of the cell divisions of the eight-cell stage blastomeres in the human embryo.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging and cell size analysis.

claim: The timing of compaction and polarization is more heterogeneous in human embryos compared to mouse embryos.
source: The results we present here indicate that the timing of compaction and polarization is more heterogeneous in human embryos as some human embryos complete compaction and polarization by the end of the eight-cell stage, while others complete these processes after the eight-cell stage.
evidence: Inferred from the variability in timing observed across human embryos.

claim: Developmental asynchronicity could be a species-specific feature of human embryo development.
source: Although such developmental asynchronicity can be a species-specific feature of human embryo development, this variability could also reflect individual differences of the embryo donors, such as genetic factors or the age of the couples.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the causes of observed variability.

claim: Variability in human embryo development could reflect individual differences of the embryo donors, such as genetic factors or the age of the couples.
source: Although such developmental asynchronicity can be a species-specific feature of human embryo development, this variability could also reflect individual differences of the embryo donors, such as genetic factors or the age of the couples.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the causes of observed variability.

claim: If embryos compact with more than eight cells, some blastomeres may adopt an inner position due to the restricted surface space.
source: Theoretically, the limited outer surface of the embryo restricts the number of outer cells (Nissen et al., 2017). In this context, if embryos compact with more than eight cells, some blastomeres may adopt an inner position due to the restricted surface space.
evidence: Theoretical reasoning based on spatial constraints and citation to literature.

claim: The limited outer surface of the embryo restricts the number of outer cells.
source: Theoretically, the limited outer surface of the embryo restricts the number of outer cells (Nissen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on embryo geometry.

claim: Already at the two-cell stage, blastomeres of the human embryo have a biased lineage allocation to either the ICM or the TE.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that already at the two-cell stage, blastomeres of the human embryo have a biased lineage allocation to either the ICM or the TE (Bizzotto et al., 2021; Custers et al., 2021), as previously shown in mouse embryos (Gardner, 2001; Piotrowska et al., 2001; Piotrowska-Nitsche et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on human and mouse embryo lineage allocation.

claim: In mouse embryos, blastomeres at the two-cell stage have a biased lineage allocation to either the ICM or the TE.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that already at the two-cell stage, blastomeres of the human embryo have a biased lineage allocation to either the ICM or the TE (Bizzotto et al., 2021; Custers et al., 2021), as previously shown in mouse embryos (Gardner, 2001; Piotrowska et al., 2001; Piotrowska-Nitsche et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mouse embryo lineage allocation.

claim: Cell polarity regulates TE differentiation in the human embryo as it does in the mouse.
source: Consistent with our findings, Gerri and colleagues showed that cell polarity regulates TE differentiation in the human embryo as it does in the mouse.
evidence: Supported by reference to another study (Gerri et al., 2020).

claim: The initiation of the expression of the TE transcription factor GATA3 is independent of cell polarization.
source: By characterizing earlier time points, our study demonstrates that the initiation of the expression of the TE transcription factor GATA3 is independent of cell polarization but that cell polarization reinforces the TE fate, which becomes established at the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Supported by data showing GATA3 expression in unpolarized cells.

claim: Cell polarization reinforces the TE fate, which becomes established at the blastocyst stage.
source: By characterizing earlier time points, our study demonstrates that the initiation of the expression of the TE transcription factor GATA3 is independent of cell polarization but that cell polarization reinforces the TE fate, which becomes established at the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Supported by data showing higher GATA3 levels in polarized cells.

claim: Activation of PLC signaling is the upstream mechanism that triggers polarization in human embryos.
source: In addition, our results also identify activation of PLC signaling as the upstream mechanism that triggers polarization in human embryos, providing mechanistic insight into human development at a stage when a crucial morphogenetic transition occurs.
evidence: Supported by RNAi and inhibitor experiments showing PLC requirement for polarization.

claim: F-actin polarization precedes PAR complex polarization in mouse and human embryos.
source: F-actin polarization precedes PAR complex polarization and it is triggered by PLC activation in mouse and human embryos.
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis of polarization markers in both species (Figure 5).

claim: F-actin polarization is triggered by PLC activation in mouse and human embryos.
source: F-actin polarization precedes PAR complex polarization and it is triggered by PLC activation in mouse and human embryos.
evidence: Supported by PLC inhibition and knockdown experiments (Figure 5).

claim: In human embryos, blastomeres initiate the expression of TE factors independently of the polarity machinery.
source: In human embryos, blastomeres initiate the expression of TE factors independently of the polarity machinery, but polarization reinforces a TE fate.
evidence: Supported by GATA3 expression analysis in polarized and unpolarized cells (Figure 5).

claim: In contrast to mouse embryos, in which inner cell generation takes place only once all blastomeres become polarized, inner cells can be observed in human embryos that are not fully polarized.
source: In contrast to mouse embryos, in which inner cell generation takes place only once all blastomeres become polarized, inner cells can be observed in human embryos that are not fully polarized, indicating mechanistic differences in the first lineage decision between the two species.
evidence: Supported by analysis of inner cell presence in relation to polarization status (Figure 5).

claim: There are mechanistic differences in the first lineage decision between mouse and human embryos.
source: In contrast to mouse embryos, in which inner cell generation takes place only once all blastomeres become polarized, inner cells can be observed in human embryos that are not fully polarized, indicating mechanistic differences in the first lineage decision between the two species.
evidence: Inferred from the differences in inner cell generation between mouse and human embryos.
